meta.title: Who really said "Many of life's failures are people who did not realize how close they were to success when they gave up"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Credited to Thomas Edison everywhere, but no primary source contains it. The earliest citation is a 2007 book claiming an 1877 date. A widely-repeated but unverified attribution.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Many of life's failures are people who did not realize how close they were to success when they gave up'?
meta.ogDescription: Everyone credits Thomas Edison, yet no contemporary source records it. The trail runs cold at a 2007 book dating it to 1877 with no evidence.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Credited to Edison across the internet — and even on the Edison Innovation Foundation’s own quote page ↗ — and it squares neatly with his documented gospel of persistence. But no contemporary source records Edison saying or writing it: the earliest citation is a 2007 children’s book that assigns it to 1877 with no supporting evidence, and Wikiquote editors removed it ↗ as unverifiable. Widely credited, but not pinned to any primary source.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: From Telegraph to Light Bulb with Thomas Edison (2007), p. 22

source.excerpt: Many of life’s failures are people who did not realize how close they were to success when they gave up.
trail: The line is credited to Edison on virtually every quote site, and even on the Edison Innovation Foundation’s quote page ↗ — but such modern pages recycle popular attributions rather than cite primary sources.

The Wikiquote talk page ↗ traces the only citation to a 2007 book that dates the line to 1877; editors noted a quote is unlikely to “survive unpublished for 130 years” and pulled it for lack of a contemporary source.
Quote Investigator ↗ has no dedicated entry for this line; its closest work traces the persistence poem “Don’t Quit” to Edgar A. Guest (1921) — a related sentiment, not this quote.
source.excerptNote: A common longer variant reads “Many of life’s failures are experienced by people who did not realize how close they were to success when they gave up” — neither wording is traceable to a document from Edison’s lifetime.

source.rightsNote: Because no primary work or first-publication date can be tied to this exact wording, its copyright status cannot be responsibly asserted. The earliest known appearance is a 2007 book — itself in copyright — but that is a citation of the quote, not evidence of an original Edison-era source.

author.name: Thomas Edison
author.heading: About Thomas Edison
author.bio: Thomas Alva Edison was one of history’s most prolific inventors, holding over a thousand US patents for devices including the phonograph, the practical incandescent light bulb, and the motion-picture camera. His public persona was built on relentless trial-and-error — famously reframing thousands of failed experiments as steps toward success — which is exactly why aphorisms about persistence gravitate to his name, whether or not the words are his.

misattribution.heading: An unverified Edison attribution
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook “magnet-name” quote: a tidy line about perseverance pinned to the world’s most famous champion of trial and error. The attribution is everywhere, but the paper trail is missing.

items.why: No source from Edison’s lifetime records this line. The only citation surfaced by Wikiquote editors ↗ is a 2007 children’s book that labels it a “statement of 1877” with no supporting evidence — 130 years after the fact — which is why the line was removed from the sourced article.
The nearly-there sentiment (“you never can tell how close you are”) is documented in Guest’s 1921 poem “Don’t Quit,” per Quote Investigator ↗. It is a cousin of this quote, not its origin.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest verdict: widely credited to Edison and in keeping with his outlook, but with no primary source ↗ — treat it as attributed, not confirmed.

context.heading: Why this sticks to Edison
lead: Edison spent decades cultivating an image of dogged persistence — the man who reportedly tried thousands of filament materials before the light bulb worked. That reputation makes his name a natural home for any well-turned line about not giving up, which is precisely how unsourced aphorisms accrete to famous inventors.

The catch is that a quote appearing only in twenty-first-century books and quote sites, with its earliest ‘source’ dating it more than a century after the fact, is a hallmark of a later coinage retrofitted to a famous name rather than a genuine Edison utterance.
context.pull: The attribution is everywhere; the primary source is nowhere.
